title: Monolith vs Microservices
text: Micro services. Micro means small, but how small exactly? And service means well, bit, does something? It's probably more helpful to understand what microservices are not, a monolith. A traditional architecture where a whole system is built as one unified self-contained application. We need concepts to live in certain areas of the software and not to leak into others. We divide the large system into smaller, manageable subsystems. We only allow a certain few interactions between boundaries by making some code internal or private, hidden away and inaccessible by the rest of the software

title: Monolith vs Microservices
text: . These subsystems are isolated modules all hosted within this large application. This architecture is called the modular monolith. We can get some clean, loosely coupled code that's easy to understand and easy to navigate. We could leave this architecture as it is, or we could host each of these independent modules as totally separate processes. These are microservices. Each service can be updated independently. We can deploy changes to one service while the others continue running

text: . These are microservices. Each service can be updated independently. We can deploy changes to one service while the others continue running. They could each run on different machines which can scale independently. Performance bottlenecks are easier to identify if we find that say one service is using lots of CPU. And if one service fails, the others can still handle requests as normal. Each service uses its own database too, which is similar benefits to the independent services

title: Monolith vs Microservices
text: . Each service uses its own database too, which is similar benefits to the independent services. They can each fail without taking the other databases down and they can scale independently. Services communicate with each other over a network using some API, whether that's HTTP requests or using a message queue. We need to ensure that we don't deploy breaking changes to an API that is being used by another service, so the boundaries between services become much more difficult to change

title: Monolith vs Microservices
text: . Network calls are much slower than the inter-process communication that was allowed before, and it usually involves writing a lot more code to handle the call. All of these constraints can feel like a bad thing, but the benefit is they formalise the boundaries between the systems. Developers are incentivised not to rely on passing information between boundaries too much, and instead build loosely coupled systems that don't depend on each other to function
